az_groom_creek.blurb: Groom Creek is a bouldering-only zone in the foothills of the Bradshaw Mountains, a short way up the highway south of Prescott at around 6,400 feet. Steel-grey, mid-grain boulders sit among tall ponderosa pines, with gravel walkways between them and mostly good landings. Problems range from overhanging jugs to slabby slopers, and the grades start at the very easiest and climb into double digits; the biggest share is easy, with a long spread through V2 to V8. The layout is complex, so expect to need a few visits to learn it. The Main Boulders hold most of the problems, and the Satellite Areas make up the rest.

ca_split_rocks_2.blurb: Split Rocks is the biggest cluster of formations in Pinto Basin, on the quieter side of Joshua Tree National Park at around 4,200 feet. The feel is noticeably different from the busier crags in the western part of the park, particularly at the more remote walls. Trad dominates by a wide margin, with a fair amount of sport, some top-rope and a few boulder problems. Grades run from 5.4 up to the low 5.12s, but most routes sit between 5.9 and 5.11, so it suits a climber with some experience. The main parts are Split Rocks West, Split Rocks East and the Approach Road Crags, with the bouldering gathered in its own small zone.

co_steamboat_springs.blurb: Steamboat Springs sits in northwestern Colorado at about 7,000 feet, and its crags are short but of good quality. Sport routes are the largest share, followed by trad, with some bouldering, top-rope and a small amount of alpine, ice and mixed. Most grades fall between 5.7 and 5.11, with fewer at 5.12, so the area is friendly to moderate climbers. The climbing is scattered over dozens of small crags and boulder zones rather than one big cliff. Rose Domes, Cougar, Hole in the Wall Canyon and Muddy Creek are among the larger ones, and Hole in the Wall adds multi-pitch trad. The town is better known for skiing, and winter is not the time to plan on climbing.

mi_lower_peninsula.blurb: Climbing in Michigan's Lower Peninsula is concentrated at Grand Ledge, where sandstone cliffs run along the Grand River in Oak Park. Because the rock is soft and brittle, climbers mostly top-rope and boulder rather than lead. Bouldering makes up the larger share, from V0 up through V10, followed by top-rope routes from about 5.7 to a hard 5.13. The south-facing cliff gets sun for most of the day and is sheltered from the wind, and it fills with climbers on nice evenings and weekends. Holds vary: the established lines are pretty good, but other stretches can be loose, so check holds carefully.

nm_capulin_canyon.blurb: Capulin Canyon lies in the Dome Wilderness of the Jemez Mountains, at roughly 7,400 feet. It is a trad area, with almost no sport, built around crack climbing on welded tuff cliffs up to about 200 feet tall. The tuff takes gear well, but it is softer than granite and its quality changes from the bottom of a cliff to the top, so expect some loose rock. Routes run from about 5.7 to 5.13, mostly in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, and the area expects a fairly experienced climber. The cliffs with the best climbing face south and there is no tree cover, so shade is gone after noon, and summers can be extremely hot. Main Cliff and Upper Wall are the biggest sections.

pa_wissahickon_valley_park.blurb: Wissahickon Valley Park holds most of the natural-rock climbing inside Philadelphia, strung along the creek through forested valley. The rock is Wissahickon schist, and most of the climbing is bouldering, with a handful of top-rope, sport and trad lines on top. Problems start at the easiest grades and run up to about V9, but most are in the V0 to V4 range. Livezey Rock is the most developed single spot, with bouldering and short top-rope lines on south-facing rock that the surrounding trees shade in the morning. Despite the city setting, the park feels fairly isolated, and its trails are busy with hikers, runners and cyclists in good weather.
